name: Oil pulling

lead: Oil pulling is the practice of swishing an edible oil, such as sesame or coconut oil, around the mouth for a period and then spitting it out. It comes from Ayurvedic tradition and has been promoted in recent years for oral hygiene, bad breath, gum health and whiter teeth.
Small trials have looked at plaque, gingivitis and bacterial counts, with mixed results. In looksmaxxing forums it is debated mainly as a whitening method, for which no study was identified.

paras: Proponents say oil 'pulls' bacteria and toxins from the mouth. A skeptic commentator cited on Wikipedia suggests any benefit is from mechanical swishing. Some oils contain compounds, such as lauric acid in coconut oil, that have been proposed to be antimicrobial.

Dental bodies describe it as unlikely to harm, though the American Dental Association says no reliable studies support it. Case reports describe exogenous lipoid pneumonia after repeated sesame oil pulling, and it is not recommended for young children because of swallowing risks.

lead: Oil pulling is a traditional practice from Ayurvedic medicine in which edible oil, commonly sesame, coconut or sunflower, is swished in the mouth and then spat out, similar to using a mouthwash [1]. Ayurvedic texts refer to it as kavala or gandusha, and it is promoted for oral hygiene, bad breath, gum health and, in modern wellness circles, tooth whitening [2][3].

Clinical research consists mostly of small trials and reviews. Some report reduced plaque, gingivitis or bacterial counts, but a 2016 systematic review found the trials small and underpowered, and the American Dental Association has said there are no reliable studies supporting the practice [1][4]. Case reports describe lipoid pneumonia after aspiration of oil [5].
infobox: Late 20th century, credited to F. Karach (per a reference summary) [2]

paras: Oil pulling is described in classical Ayurvedic texts and is part of traditional daily oral routines [2]. A reference summary credits Ukrainian physician F. Karach with a modern revival in the early 1990s, and a 2008 book by Bruce Fife with popularising it in the West; it was later promoted by wellness media and celebrities [2].

On looksmax.org the practice is discussed both as a breath and oral-hygiene habit and as a whitening method. Some posters describe improved breath after a few days, and others describe it as ineffective for whitening and suggest professional whitening or strips instead [6][7].

Wikipedia reports that the article's sources contain no high-quality research on oil pulling, and that the American Dental Association says there are no reliable studies supporting it, while the Canadian Dental Association said in 2014 it was not convinced of benefits but sensed it would do no harm [1].

Reviews of coconut oil pulling and of oil pulling for oral hygiene have summarised trials on plaque, gingivitis and microbial counts [8][9]. A reference summary reports that meta-analyses show modest and inconsistent results, with chlorhexidine generally superior for plaque [2].

Two cases of exogenous lipoid pneumonia associated with repeated sesame oil pulling have been reported [5]. A reference summary says the practice is not recommended for children under five because of swallowing risks [2].

Small randomised trials have tested oil pulling on plaque-induced gingivitis (sesame oil compared with chlorhexidine) [10], on gingivitis with coconut oil [11], on Streptococcus mutans counts [12], and on halitosis [13]. Systematic review of coconut oil pulling is available [8]. No clinical trial of tooth whitening was identified.

lore.intro: Oil pulling is discussed on looksmax.org as a low-cost breath and teeth routine, often compared with hydrogen peroxide rinses and professional whitening [6][7].

claims.claim: Oil pulling improves breath and removes bacteria

timeline.event: Physician F. Karach presents oil pulling at a Ukrainian conference, according to a reference summary [2].
Bruce Fife publishes a book on oil pulling therapy [2].
Celebrity discussion of oil pulling and the Canadian Dental Association comment [1][2].
